The pool holds the smell of chlorine like a held breath, and Aaron is in the water at the same hour she is, again, until it stops being a coincidence and becomes a fact she has to decide what to do with. Within a fortnight he is in her house, and neither of them says why he came looking for a stranger's widow in the first place.

Lena keeps the drawings on the wall behind the kitchen table even after she has started again, in the bathroom of a bar with the door locked, then in the house, at that table, with the paper curling at the corners. She does not remember deciding to use. It felt like starting a job.

Wes cleans rooms at a motel four hundred miles from anywhere that knows him. Released early on somebody's recommendation, he got as far as the gate, saw the family waiting, and kept walking. The Bible verses are still on his forearms; he doesn't look at them much now.

A doctor once told a mathematician named Aaron that his heart had weeks left in it, and his wife Della, out of the house a year already, sat across from him with a clinic form, asking him to sign while he still could. What is in the freezer is all there will ever be, she said. He did not say yes or no. He signed.

In an operating theatre a chest opens and a heart that was beating an hour ago in somebody else goes into it. Aaron wakes in the night and can breathe, and lies there listening to the borrowed thing going. He cannot stop thinking about whose it was. He pays a man in a car park to find out, is told it is against every rule there is, and pays him anyway.

Wes was born again once, working a job, coaching boys on Saturdays, testifying to whoever sat still long enough. His wife Nita watched the certainty in him like weather coming.

A pickup came through a crossing wrong and took a man and two children off their feet. It went on a hundred yards, stopped, sat with the engine running, backed up a little, and then went. In a hospital corridor Lena was told first about her husband and then, while she was still absorbing that, about both girls.

Aaron tells Lena about the heart in her kitchen, badly. She puts him out that night with everything he brought. Four days later she asks him back, and he comes.

Wes walked up the steps of a police station on his own once and told the desk sergeant everything, how far he'd driven after, and was back inside within the month.

Aaron leaves Della and tells her he doesn't want the child she's trying to conceive. She tells him the true thing, that he is spending a life somebody else paid for, and he has no answer for that because by then he already knows whose life it was, though she doesn't.

Lena used to do the school run, keep the garden, sit at that table with two girls and a husband who adored her, in a house with a fixed rate on it. That was before. Or it feels like before, though nothing in the telling insists on it.

She says she cannot go on breathing in the same country as the man who did it, and keeps saying it until it's the only thing in the house. Aaron buys a pistol from a man in a lock-up.

Behind the motel he gets Wes against a wall in the dark and cannot make his hand finish it. The shot goes somewhere that will not kill. He tells him to get up and run.

Wes follows them back to their room instead, bleeding through his shirt, and stands in the doorway asking to be finished. Aaron turns the gun around and puts it into his own chest.

They get him into the car with the horn down. The heart that came out of the crossing stops on a table in a hospital that has already seen all three of these lives pass through it in one form or another. Wes goes home to the family he walked out on. Lena goes home alone, carrying something that has not yet a name, from a freezer, from a signature, from a wife who asked a dying man to leave behind more than a heart.

The alarm was already going before they were fully out the door, and Mr. Ash fired through the windscreen and out both side windows while Danny sat beside him with his ears ringing, the car fishtailing down a street that was not the street they had planned to be on. That was the whole job undone in under a minute.

He remembered, lying on the warehouse ramp with Ash's hands pressed against his stomach and his own blood running warm under his back, how Pruitt had made him say the anecdote about the dogs and the drugs and the public toilet over and over in that grey little room until it stopped sounding rehearsed and started sounding lived. You have to remember it, Pruitt said, not recite it. He hadn't understood what that meant until he was telling it to Bram and Cal and Ash in the bar, timing the laugh, and watching the boss decide he was worth having. He'd walked out with a name he hadn't chosen and no colour of his own.

Ash was saying nobody dies here today, nobody dies, and Danny wanted to tell him that was the same lie in a different room but he didn't have the breath.

He'd taken it in the stomach from a woman he'd dragged out of her own car, her hand already inside the door pocket, and he had shot her before the door was shut, and driven himself here bleeding and screaming with Ash beside him, gun still hot from the getaway. Before any of that there had been a breakfast, eight men in black suits arguing about what a pop song was really about and whether the woman pouring coffee deserved anything for it, nobody using a name that was theirs — that had been the last easy morning, after Bram handed out the tree names in his office and Birch spent a full minute complaining that his was the worst of the lot. Ren had walked into that same office days earlier straight off a stretch he could have shortened by talking, and Bram had paid him for his silence with an envelope and a seat on the job.

Birch arrived clean, furious, laying out the timings — the police on the pavement before the alarm even sounded — and went out to bury the diamonds where nobody watching him could see, saying there was an informer in the room and he meant to find him.

Then Ren came in unhurried, complaining about all the shouting, and opened his boot and dragged out a young patrolman named Doyle with his hands bound. He left him alone with him for a while, found an oldie on the radio, danced a few steps, and cut the man's ear off before dousing him in petrol.

That was when Danny, on the floor with nothing left to lose, emptied his gun into Ren. Then he told Doyle what he was — a police officer — and that there were men waiting outside in cars for Bram. Cal came back before rescue did, listened to the story, decided it held, and shot Doyle himself to close it.

Bram arrived last, looked down at the man bleeding on the concrete, and said this is the one. Ash put his gun on his own boss rather than believe it.

All three fired. Bram and Cal went down and stayed down; Ash took a wound that left him on his knees, still breathing, still refusing.

Danny told him then, because the man had earned it and there was no more use in the lie — that he was police, that it had all been exactly what Bram said. Ash dragged himself upright, put the barrel to his own head as the doors came in and the lights came with them, and was cut down kneeling, the truth arriving in him a half-second before the bullets did, Danny already gone beside him, the anecdote about the dogs and the bathroom the last thing that had ever been entirely his own.

THE WATCH

The boy sat very still while the man just returned from years in a foreign prison put the gold watch into his hands. "Your father kept it hidden through everything," the man said. "He wanted you to have it more than he wanted his own name back." Denny turned it over and over, feeling its weight, understanding for the first time that his father was truly gone, and that this small heavy thing had cost more than he could yet measure.

Years later he wore it every day, felt for it on the bedside table each morning without looking, until the night he asked Marielle in a motel room off the highway whether she'd packed it and watched her face fall. It was still sitting on the table in a flat that men were surely watching. "It's just a watch," she said, and he told her it was the only thing his father had ever managed to keep. He went back for it, let himself in, found it exactly where it had been left — and found Rollo coming out of the bathroom at the same moment, a submachine gun on the counter nearer to Denny's hand than to its owner's. He put the watch on before he left the building.

It had first come to danger, in a way, in Otis's bar, weeks earlier, before any of this — Denny at the counter being paid to go down in the fifth, the watch on his wrist while Otis counted bills into his palm and told him which round. He didn't go down. He won, and did more than win, and was gone in a taxi before the crowd worked out what they'd seen, the watch ticking against the wheel of the cab.

Rollo and Marcus, meanwhile, had their own morning, unconnected to any watch, crossing the city arguing about foreign hamburgers, then standing in a corridor debating whether a foot massage was worth a man's life, before Marcus recited scripture over a young man named Tobin and they shot him for Otis and took his briefcase. A fourth man came screaming out of a bathroom and put a whole revolver's worth of rounds into the wall behind them without touching either one. Marcus called it a miracle. In the car afterward his gun went off by accident and took the top of Del's head off, and they drove the ruined car to Warren's garage, where a soft-voiced fixer had them hosed down in the yard and dressed like students. In borrowed shorts they carried the briefcase into Otis's bar — the same morning, in fact, that Denny was being paid to dive.

The briefcase had one more stop before Otis. In a coffee shop that morning a couple decided over eggs that nobody ever robbed a restaurant, and were up on the booth seats with a pistol before the plates were cleared. Marcus let the gun be held on him, handed over his own wallet, told them what he'd decided the morning's miracle meant, and let them walk out the door with nothing but his goodwill.

Rollo, later, drove out to Kip's for heroin and shot up at the kitchen table, then took Otis's wife Nadia dancing at a themed restaurant where they won the contest barefoot. Back at Kip's, Nadia found the bag in his coat, mistook it for something else, and had to be brought back from blue with a needle to the heart on the living-room floor.

After the fight, after the flat, after the watch was back on his wrist, Denny drove into Otis crossing the street with a paper bag in his arms, and both men ended up dragged into a pawnshop basement. Denny broke free, and at the door he stopped, took a sword off the wall, and went back down for the man who'd been hunting him. Otis called them square, on condition he never returned.

He collected Marielle from the motel, put her on a stolen motorcycle, the watch ticking quietly against his wrist, and rode out of the city they were never going back to.

The nurse had told Nash to come to Silvermount at the end of the week, when the estate lawyers would be finished with the inventory, and so Nash spent the days before that in a screening room watching nine minutes of Emmett Rusk's public life run over and over: the palace going up floor by floor, the two front-page weddings, the election night with its six-column FRAUD headline, the collapse. The reel explained the shape of the man and none of the inside of him. It ended, as everyone knew it would, without saying what the dying man had meant by "Bluebell."

He started with the second wife because she had the most reason to know and the most reason to refuse. He found her at four in the afternoon in a seaside club, a glass in front of her that was not her first, and she told him to get out before he had finished his second sentence.

So he went back further than she was willing to go. He read Barrow's memoir first, in a marble library that still smelled of new paint, and there it was — a mother at a kitchen table in a mining town, signing her boy over the moment a defaulted lodger's worthless deed turned out to sit on an enormous seam. A father objecting from the doorway and being ignored. A boy who did not go quietly: he put a sled into the banker's stomach hard enough to sit him down, and was taken east anyway, that same evening, as if the fight had never happened.

Marsh remembered the day the fortune came to him whole, at twenty-five, and Emmett looking down the list of holdings and choosing, of everything, a newspaper that lost money every month, because he thought it might be fun. Marsh remembered the bed moved into the office, the statement of principles set on the front page over his own signature, and then the party — the whole staff of the rival paper hired away with money alone, a brass band, a line of dancers, Emmett dancing in the middle of it like a boy who had gotten exactly what he wanted.

Devlin, when Nash found him, had a lot to say about the wife who came before Nora — the trip abroad for statuary, the wedding on every front page but his own, and then the breakfasts, longer and longer apart, until husband and wife sat at either end of a table reading rival newspapers, one of which he owned. Devlin remembered the mud-splashed coat and the shopgirl laughing back at a chemist's window, and the secret rooms, and how the party boss Halloran had walked the wife up those stairs ten days before the vote and offered a trade, and how Emmett had told him to get out of the building rather than be told what to do. Devlin remembered asking for a transfer the week the marriage and the election died together, and being talked out of leaving — for a while.

Nora, seen a second time, sober this time, told him about the singing lessons she never wanted, the house bought to make people believe she had a voice, the unbearable debut, and how Devlin had gotten too drunk to finish the review and Emmett had finished it himself, in the same cruel direction, printed it, and dismissed his oldest friend for the sentence he'd completed. She told him about the poison, and about being allowed, finally, to stop only because she had nearly died first. She told him about Silvermount — the ceilings too high to heat, the crates never opened, the jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall the size of a station — and the black-beach picnic where nothing was enjoyed by anybody, and the morning she packed regardless of what he told her she could not do.

Colm, the butler, was the one who had watched him tear the abandoned bedroom apart with his hands and stop at a glass globe full of snow, and carry it past the mirrors, murmuring the one word to no one.

Nash closed his notebook in the empty hall at Silvermount, workmen shovels going through crates behind him, and said, mostly to himself, that no single word ever explained a life. Below, in the furnace room, a small sled marked BLUEBELL went into the fire with the rest of the unwanted things, and nobody there knew enough to stop them.

He wakes late, headache behind his eyes, a strange flat feeling in the flat, like a room that has had furniture taken out of it. Nothing in his head that wasn't there two years ago. That is what he thinks, though he has no way of knowing it. He gets up, dresses for work, and at the platform something makes him board the other train instead. He cannot say why. He rides it to the end of the line, walks out onto frozen sand, and finds a woman with dyed hair already standing there.

Two technicians let themselves into his flat the night before, capped him while he slept, and worked room by room through a map built from a hairslide, a mug, a torn page. One of them quietly pocketed the bag of keepsakes. Inside his own skull Tobias stood in the worst of it, the shouting, the dent in the car, the door, and watched the walls fall away while he was still in them. When the machine reached the memories he loved, he ran, carrying her into places she had never been, a childhood kitchen, under a table, anywhere the map didn't reach.

On the beach she says nothing about any of it, of course; she only says she wondered if anyone would come. They drive back into the city talking too easily for two strangers. Outside her building she asks him up for a drink as though it were the second time, not the first.

Two on the outside had been drinking his beer and dancing on his bed in their underwear while the map on the screen quietly stopped meaning anything, and neither noticed for a long while. That is what was happening on the far side of the wall from the kitchen he'd invented for her.

In her flat, she pours the drinks. Something in him keeps almost saying a name he doesn't have.

The director was called out at three in the morning to put the machine back on its rails. In the hallway the receptionist kissed him, and his wife, arriving a step behind, told her precisely why she'd always felt that way about him, and why she couldn't remember it. Rosa stood very still and understood what had been done to her.

Ivy asks him to stay for a second drink. He says yes before he's decided to.

The last surviving room was the shore house, the night they met, glass still cold on the boards. In the doorway, before it went, she told him to walk out and come and find her at the coast. That was the whole instruction. It was enough.

Weeks earlier — though he does not know this either — he had gone to the bookshop to make things right and found her looking at him like a customer, laughing at a boy behind the counter. Two friends had handed him a form letter afterward, the same one sent to everyone she'd ever known, and he'd taken it straight to the clinic and demanded the same erasure for himself, that afternoon if possible. He had filled two bags with everything of hers he owned so the machine would know where to cut.

Now, in her stairwell, months later, two envelopes arrive on the same morning, sent by a receptionist who quit and emptied the filing cabinets on her way out. Files. Forms. Tapes of their own voices explaining what they'd wanted removed and why.

They sit on the stairs and listen. Two years compressed into an hour of tape: the ice on the river, steam on the windows of the noodle house, the drive-in with the sound turned low, and then the same rooms turning, her drinking, his silences, the dent in the car, the finishing blow neither of them can take back even now. Ivy runs down two flights and out the door. He waits. She comes back up.

Before any of it — before the clinics, the tapes, the two trains going opposite ways through the same names — there was only a beach full of strangers and a man with nothing to say to anyone, and a woman with dyed hair, and a window they broke together in an empty house to get out of the cold.

They decide, on the stairs, with everything now known, to do it again anyway.

Martin sits on the end of a motel bed he does not remember taking and tells the story down the phone the way he always tells it: the claimant with the soft voice, the tests, the denial, the case that isn't his. The caller listens like he already knows how it ends.

A year earlier, give or take, Roy walks him through evidence spread on a car hood and says they've got him, the second man, out past the edge of town. Martin fires once and it's over, and within minutes he's asking who they were looking for.

The caller feeds him a name over the line — Gil Marsh, a dealer, an address, a time. Martin writes it down like scripture.

Before that, in the rented room that is not this room, Martin tapes photographs to the wall and captions them in block capitals, six facts under his skin already, more to come.

In a basement with water on the floor, Martin beats a man half his size and finishes it with a belt, then takes the picture.

Before the room, before the tattoos, there was the bathroom: two men through the door at night, a shot fired across his wife's body, glass folding in on him, and after that nothing new would ever stay.

Gil whispers a name that means nothing to Martin, who takes the dead man's suit, his keys, his car, and drives away wearing someone else's life.

In a field, once, Martin burned a hairbrush and a stack of paperbacks, waiting to feel the ending arrive. It never did.

Roy finds him in the derelict building and lays it flat: the dealer was nobody, the revenge already happened a year ago, and the story Martin recites to strangers is not a case file. It's his house.

Before the field there was a living room, and a wife with diabetes who moved her own watch forward and asked for the injection again, and again, believing there had to be a limit to what he'd forget.

Rather than hold what Roy has given him, Martin burns Gil's photographs, writes *he is lying to you* across Roy's picture, and copies a license plate off the car outside.

Before the living room, an insurance office, and a soft-spoken man named Elias Prine failing test after test while Martin decided, behind a desk, that none of it was real.

Martin has the plate driven into his thigh under five other facts, and does not remember writing the note that told him to.

At her bar, Corinne watches a stranger walk in wearing Gil's suit, and has the staff spit in his beer before it reaches him.

She clears every pen from the house, says the things that will make him swing, and comes back bruised, blaming a man called Vance.

Martin waits in a motel bathroom in the dark, takes Vance down as he comes through the door, and drives him out past the town line with a gun in his ribs.

Corinne runs the plate through a friend at the registry and slides a printout across the table: Roy Mercer, in full.

Martin brings Roy out to the same derelict building, walks him into the room, and puts one through his head, then photographs what's left, certain, at last, that the note was right — never knowing that the note, like everything else he carries, was something he was only ever told to believe.

I hadn't slept in six months when I found out that grief buys sleep cheap, if it isn't yours. Four evenings a week I sat in folding chairs in church halls, listening to men and women describe diseases eating them from the inside, and I cried for them like they were mine, and I went home and slept like the dead. It worked until Ada Vey started showing up too, smoking through the meditation, obviously faking it, and once I could see the lie in her I could see it in myself, and the sleep stopped.

I met the man who fixed that on a night flight. Soap salesman, bad suitcase, better opinions. Talked for forty minutes about how everything either of us owned had been chosen for us by someone else. I kept his card without knowing why.

Here is a thing I already knew then, though I wouldn't understand it for a long time: at the bottom of a service stairwell in a tower full of debt records, I would put a gun in my own mouth and fire it through my cheek, because the man walking me down those stairs was going to kill me otherwise, and he was going to kill me because he was me.

My flat went up while I was on a trip — windows on the pavement, the catalogue furniture gone with them. I stood at a phone box and called the salesman instead of anyone sensible, and he took me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing and no questions.

Outside a bar he asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We went at each other on the tarmac until neither of us could stand, laughing. It became a Tuesday thing in a cellar, then a waiting list, then rules read aloud at the door.

Ada overdosed and rang, and he went and brought her back to the house, and for weeks the two of them were audible through every floor while I lay rigid downstairs hating it.

He was boiling fat lifted from a cosmetic surgery clinic on the kitchen stove, cutting it, wrapping it, selling it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He tipped lye on the back of my hand once and held it there, wouldn't let me go into the cave or count my breath, made me stay in the minute with the burn. I still have that mark. I would still have it, wrapped in gauze, at a high window months later, holding a woman's hand while buildings came down outside in order, apologetic shaven men having just delivered her to me and gone.

I used my own beaten face as evidence and blackmailed my employer into paying me to disappear. The cellar became an organisation with a name — Havoc — and the house filled with shaven boys who slept on the floor and went out at night to break things belonging to companies. Then he took both hands off the wheel on a wet road and let the car roll, and when I came round in the ditch he wasn't there and wasn't anywhere.

Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill still in his hand, and I started trying to shut down what I'd made. I flew city to city and found the same cellar under every bar, the same rules on the same wall, and men who looked up and called me by his name.

In a motel room, with flight records and receipts spread over the bed, it went together: one body, one bank account, one man asleep and the same man awake. I called Ada and asked, badly, whose bed she'd been in. His, she said, obviously, and what was wrong with me.

I found the vans under the towers, wired and timed, holding every record of who owed what. And then the stairwell, and the gun that was in his hand and was in mine, and the trigger, and my own cheek opening around the shot.

She was brought to the window afterward. We held hands while the towers went down one after another, in order, exactly as planned, with or without me.

Above the noise, at the open window, the old man went on talking as though the sirens below were part of his argument rather than an interruption of it. "Nothing survives," he said. "Not stone, not paper, not the two of you standing there thinking you'll remember this exactly as it happened. You won't. You'll remember a version, and then a version of the version, until there's nothing left but the fact that something occurred." The younger man said nothing. Below them the blue light kept turning over the wet street, patient as a tide.

It had turned there only minutes before, when the police carried Cort and Jonah out through the crowd with their hands cuffed behind them, one shouting about his arm, the other silent, his knuckles split and swelling. The crowd parted for them the way crowds do, already forgetting.

Before that there had been the club itself, the extinguisher taken off the wall, the sound of it landing and landing after there was any reason to keep swinging. A few feet off, watching with the same flat interest as everyone else, stood the man they had actually been looking for, unremarked, unhurt.

Before that: the wrong man, taken by the elbow, his arm turned until it came apart in Cort's hand like something badly made.

Before that: two men peeling off a doorway, offering a name for money, a nod down toward a basement door with light leaking under it.

Before that: the ambulance. Cort and Jonah coming out of the party still half-laughing at something, and stopping, because there was a trolley on the pavement and a blanket and a face on it they both knew.

Before that, in the underpass, tile light and the smell of piss and drains, a man they would later learn to call the Adder holding a woman by the hair and explaining something to her with his fist, and Lise walking in on it because she would not cross four lanes of headlights to avoid it. When he turned on her instead she didn't have time to be surprised. A man at the far end of the tunnel looked, thought about it, and left.

Before that: the party, its heat and spilled drink, Cort past the point of being any fun, working the room while she watched him do it and then didn't watch anymore. She got her coat and went.

Before that: the train, the three of them swaying in the carriage, arguing happily about sex and about how much he'd already had, the kind of argument that expects to happen again tomorrow, that assumes there will be a tomorrow.

Before that: a Sunday in the park, sprinklers turning over the grass, children shrieking through the spray, Lise on her side with a book she wasn't really reading, one hand flat on her stomach as if listening for something.

Before that: the bathroom, the stick in both hands, and her smiling at it alone before she'd told anyone at all.

Before that, the morning it all traced back to, thin light through the curtains, Cort's arm heavy across her, the three of them easy with each other the way people are before anything has gone wrong. She told him about the dream again — the tunnel, red-lit, that she kept walking into and never reached the end of — and he said something about Jonah, something about her taste in men before him, and she said something back, and they lay there a long time not needing to move.

None of that survived, the old man might have said, except as this: a street full of light, a woman on a trolley, two men taken away in handcuffs, and somewhere above it a window open to the noise, a voice explaining, patiently, that nothing lasts, as if the explaining itself might.

Nadir stood at the gun-shop counter with Sahar beside him to translate, and the dealer behind the glass did an impression of his accent while he filled out the form, for the benefit of nobody. Nadir took the box and the pistol and left with his daughter, and neither of them was smiling.

Later—months later, though no one watching that morning could have known it—a small girl would come running off a porch into her father's arms just as that same pistol went off in the dark, and nothing would happen to her, because the box Sahar had actually bought that day, quietly, while her father argued with the clerk about the price, was the box that does nothing. She never told him. He would decide, standing there with smoke and no blood anywhere, that the child was an angel sent to spare him. That was still ahead of them both.

Two young men, Trey and Kwame, walked up a restaurant pavement discussing who might be watching them, then produced pistols and took a prosecutor named Halstead's car from him and his wife on the kerb. Paula stood on the pavement shaking. Within days a locksmith named Mateo came to fit new locks on the Halstead house, and Paula told her husband, loudly, in the man's hearing, that the tattooed one would be selling their keys to his friends by morning.

Mateo went from there to Nadir's shop, fitted the lock, and warned him the door itself needed replacing. Nadir heard a man inventing a second job for himself and threw him out. The door came off its hinges within the week. The insurer read the file and declined, citing the warning he'd refused.

A patrolman named Boyle pulled over a couple, the Hobarts, for nothing, and searched Renee with his hand where it didn't need to go while her husband Clay stood three feet off and said nothing. His partner Voss went to their commander the next morning and said he couldn't ride with the man anymore, and got the transfer by calling it a stomach problem, and thought that settled something.

It didn't. Boyle sat across a desk from a clerk named Delia Frank pleading for his father's treatment, was refused, and lost his temper entirely. And it was the same Boyle who, weeks after that, crawled into a wrecked car hanging upside down on a slip road with fuel running toward flame, and got Renee's belt undone, and pulled her out — the hand that had assaulted her being the hand that saved her life.

Trey and Kwame, still driving Halstead's car, ran down a shopkeeper named Pham between two parked vans, argued about it for two streets, and left him breathing outside a hospital. Clay was later stopped mid-carjacking of his own car by four officers who'd been told it was stolen, and it was Voss — the one who'd wanted out — who walked into the middle of that and talked them down. Clay drove off afterward with Trey crouched in the passenger seat, and three miles on put him out on the verge without a word.

It was after that, alone on the road, that Trey found Pham's van packed with people who had been paid for, and drove them to the docks instead of selling them, giving them what was in his pocket.

Voss picked up a hitchhiker in the rain not long after, misread a hand going to a pocket, and shot him twice, and burned the car. The hitchhiker was Kwame. A detective named Reece was called to the body by the roadside and stopped walking when he recognized the shoes. His mother, told at her kitchen table, said only that she had asked him a hundred times to go and look and he never once went.

Paula fell down her own stairs with no one home, and in the ambulance told her housekeeper Alba that she was the only friend she had.

The first snow came over the city that winter. At a junction two cars touched, and both drivers got out shouting before either had looked at the damage.

TIGRE

The dog came off the street already knowing how to kill something bigger than itself. Ruben watched it happen in a yard behind the crowded house, and within a month it was going into a ring twice a week, coming out every time. His mother kept the peace among four adults and a baby, Nestor beat his wife Alma in the kitchen and Ruben pressed her to run, all of it under one roof with the dog. He hid the fight money in the wardrobe until the money and the wife and the child were gone with his brother, taken by the man he'd paid two thugs to hurt. Nestor went into a bank later with a scarf over his face and came out on the floor of it, and at the funeral Alma told Ruben no and meant it.

The dog outlived that whole house. In the ring one night the promoter Chaco, down too much, put a pistol into its side, and Ruben went over the rope with a knife and ran with his friend Pipo, the dog bleeding across the back seat. The truck came through a junction at speed and took the side out of a small car. A vagrant pushing a scrap cart stood in the smoke, looked at the wrecks, and lifted the bleeding dog out and walked off with it, leaving the people to the people.

His name was Cardo. He fed the dog by hand in a yard full of strays until it slept against him and followed him into the street mornings. That gentleness sat oddly beside the rest of his life: a killer for hire, a man who'd stood a long way back at his own wife's burial among people who thought he'd been dead twenty years, and then followed his grown daughter Perla home through three streets to stand outside her building doing nothing. He had a contract from a man named Elian to kill Elian's own half-brother Sergio, half paid in advance behind a church. Instead of finishing it he chained Sergio to a bed frame in the empty kennels. He came home another day to find the whole pack dead in the yard and the rottweiler standing over them with its muzzle wet, and he held a gun to its head a long time and could not fire it. Later he brought Elian face to face with the brother he'd hired him to kill, set a loaded pistol on the floor between them, and left with money from both, having handed the decision back to the men who wanted it made for them.

Somewhere across the city, in a different house, none of this mattered. A model named Celine had been moved by her lover Hector into a flat that faced her own billboard, and when a small car was hit at a junction it was hers, and Tigre's blood was already gone from the scene by the time she woke in hospital asking after her lapdog Chispa, lost somewhere in the new apartment. All night the helicopters went over, low and steady, spraying the fruit fly out of the trees and the poison down onto everyone's washing, and no one in the city slept quite the same after that hum passed over their particular roof.

Under one of those roofs, Neil Hartigan buttoned a shirt for the second time while Bess worked in her studio until the last possible minute, both of them mildly dreading the guest list they'd already committed to.

Across town, Otto the baker took an order from a woman named Elaine — a cake, a name and an age written on a card, ready Monday, please collect it promptly. The boy's name was Charlie.

On his way to school not long after, Charlie stepped off a kerb into the path of a waitress named Rhona, hurrying somewhere else. He got up, said he was fine, refused a lift, and walked the rest of the way home insisting on it.

He did not stay fine. He went to sleep on the sofa that evening and did not wake up properly, and after that there was a hospital room with a machine in it, and Grant and Elaine taking shifts in a chair. Into that silence walked Duff, Grant's father, unseen for years, who filled the quiet with a confession about a woman from decades back, because he could not think what else to give his son.

Because nobody had collected the cake, and nobody had paid for it, Otto — bad at being ignored — started ringing the Rill house at two in the morning to say the boy's name into the receiver.

Elsewhere, in the same spread of poisoned night, Cheryl talked strange men through their fantasies from her living room, folding nappies, while her husband Stu sat three feet away going quietly incandescent. That same fury sent him out with three friends to the river, where they found a young woman face down in the shallows. Rather than end the weekend, they tied a line around her ankle to keep her from drifting and fished on for two more days before telling a soul. When Vern's wife Iris heard the story as it was told at the pub, she stopped wiping off her clown makeup halfway through, sponge in hand, disgusted at what her husband had been willing to fish beside.

The helicopters had gone over the club too, where Vida sang nightly to a room mostly talking through her, and over the house where her daughter Bee practiced cello alone into an empty room. And over the Rowe house, where Officer Rowe, needing an alibi for his lie to Peg, drove the family dog to the far side of the valley and left it there, telling her it must have got over the fence. His mistress Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot himself, found out about her new man and answered by sawing her furniture to pieces in an afternoon.

Meanwhile Ike and Dot, house-sitting the Hartigans' good address, painted each other up as corpses and photographed themselves lying dead in the hall, laughing.

That night at the dinner party the Hartigans had been dreading, Bess told the table about a modelling session years ago, and then about the affair that followed it, and Neil set his glass down very carefully and made a scene of the whole evening.

By morning the machine keeping Charlie alive was switched off. That afternoon, Grant and Elaine went to the bakery to shout at Otto about the calls, and instead found themselves sitting down while he put warm bread in front of them and grieved with them for a boy whose birthday cake he had made and never delivered.

Not long after, Bee came home to find her mother asleep in the chair as always. She walked out to the garage, pulled the door down, and started the car.

And in the hills above the city, at a picnic, a young woman said some ordinary wrong thing to Stu, who had been carrying the river inside him ever since, and he answered her with a rock.

That evening the ground shook for eleven seconds. By the late bulletin, the tremor, the deaths, the wrecked furniture, and the woman finally found in the river had all been folded together into the same three minutes of news, indistinguishable, already turning into weather.

Solly Two Coats walked out of the diamond house dressed as a pilgrim, his crew shuffling beside him in borrowed piety, and nobody at the northern port so much as blinked at the stone leaving in his coat. Marv's voice came down a bad line from overseas that same week, flat and impatient: bring it straight over, he said, and don't stop to admire it.

Grigor the Nail, who liked to have his fingers in every pocket in the city, told Solly about a bookmaker's shop worth a flutter, and in the same breath told the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno that the same shop was worth robbing, though he never mentioned that to Solly.

Across town, the promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam out to the travellers' camp to buy a caravan, a simple errand that ended with Sam flat on the grass, put there by a bare-knuckle man named Finn who didn't like being haggled with. Halloway now had no fighter for Coldstone's fixed bout, so he put Finn in instead and swore to the gang boss that Finn would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed in the city, left the real stone with the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and carried an empty-handed case to the bookmaker's to lay a bet on the fight he'd heard about. Ike, Benno and a third man, Tulley, bungled the job hopelessly, grabbing Solly's arm and his case in the panic and fleeing from the very man who'd sent them, Grigor himself giving chase through the alleys.

In the ring, Finn ignored every instruction and put his man down in the first round, costing Coldstone a fortune and Halloway a beating of a different kind.

Marv, arriving to find his cousin and his diamond both gone, hired a bounty hunter named Ledge, a man who tracked stones by tracking fools. Grigor, meanwhile, had Solly in a back room and cut off his arm to force the case open, only to find it empty — the stone long gone to Hersch.

Coldstone fed what was left of Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby exactly what would happen to them if the rematch went wrong too.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers to a car on a quiet street, shot it to pieces, and took Ike, Benno, and the diamond they'd since recovered from Hersch under duress.

Halloway and Digby relayed Coldstone's threat to Finn, who agreed to go down in the fourth — and that same night Coldstone's men burned Finn's mother alive in her caravan, turning a business arrangement into blood debt.

Grigor, still hunting the stone, ambushed Ledge's car on a city road. The gunfire left Ledge, Grigor, and Benno all dead in the wreckage, and the diamond loose on the seat between them. Tulley, the only one of the original robbers still breathing, slipped away from the carnage with nothing but a stray dog that had, weeks earlier, swallowed the very diamond everyone had been dying for.

At the rematch, Finn waited exactly as long as he'd promised, to the fourth round, and then knocked his man cold — while the travellers, avenging Finn's mother, cut down Coldstone's men seat by seat through the crowd. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone alone afterward and shot him where he stood; by morning the travellers had packed up and vanished as though they'd never come.

Weeks later, a pet shop handed in a stray dog that coughed up, of all things, a diamond, and it was Halloway and Digby, of everyone who had bled and died chasing it, who ended up holding the stone that had started with a pilgrim's disguise in a northern port.

Emlyn stood in Wilder's sitting room with his coat still on, and said it plainly: he had known for four years. Odile had told him on the trip abroad, in the hotel with the letter waiting at the desk, and he had never much cared for Wilder's prose either, in the letters or out of them. Wilder had summoned him that same evening, alarmed, wanting at last the conversation both of them had spent years arranging not to have, and here it was, arriving too easily, without the violence he had braced for.

He had been summoned because of a detail Odile let slip in a bar two years after the rooms closed — that Emlyn had been quietly publishing a writer Wilder represented, a man they both privately despised. That single fact, dropped between drinks, had made the whole architecture of what Wilder believed suddenly unstable. Before that, in the same bar, she had told him her marriage was over, that she had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband, as though confession were a thing that could happen only once, freshly, and change everything on delivery.

Before that had come the closing of the rooms — no discovery, no scene, simply linen and plates divided between two people who had grown tired of maintaining a household that asked more of them than the affair itself did. Before that, dinners at Emlyn and Odile's table where the two men talked of racquets and schoolboy sport until she had no part in it at all, her own dining room turned into a country she couldn't enter. Before that, the long drunken lunch at the restaurant where Emlyn baited Wilder about contemporary fiction with a viciousness Wilder mistook for taste rather than knowledge.

Before that, Odile going back to the rented rooms and saying nothing whatever about the trip, letting the afternoon pass exactly as the others had, so that Wilder's ignorance could go on a little longer as if it were peace. Before that, in the hotel abroad, her confession, and Emlyn's strange, controlled reply — that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife. Before that, the letter itself, held at the desk in a hand Emlyn recognized, the first crack through which the whole thing entered the marriage.

Before that, further back still, Odile announcing she was carrying her husband's child, and the two of them deciding, in the rented rooms, that the affair would simply continue underneath the pregnancy, unaltered. Before that, the establishing of the rooms themselves — linen, crockery, the ordinary furniture of a second life laid over the first. And before all of it, the party at Emlyn's house, upstairs from the noise of other people's drinking, Wilder telling Odile how lovely she was, in the home of the man whose friendship he was already spending.

Now, in Wilder's sitting room, all of it stood revealed as having run the other way from how Wilder had lived it. He had thought himself the one holding the secret; he had thought Odile's bar-confession the first real reckoning; he had thought the restaurant lunch was simply Emlyn in an ugly mood. Instead Emlyn had carried the knowledge the whole time, silent through racquets and sport, silent through wine, silent at his own table while his wife sat outside the conversation she had caused.

"You might have said something," Wilder told him, though it came out without much conviction, more grief than accusation.

"I did," Emlyn said. "For four years. You simply weren't listening in the right rooms."

He said it without cruelty, almost kindly, the way a man closes an account that has been open too long. Then he asked, as if it were the only remaining question worth asking, whether Wilder still had any of the letters, and whether they were as bad as he remembered.

He has always known the hour of his death, and so he tells it first, or last, or in the middle, because on his planet, the one he was taken to see, all of that is the same violence done to a single fixed thing. He will be shot by a beam weapon after a lecture, an old man in a hall full of strangers, and he has known it since a boy in a prison camp swore vengeance on him for a death he did not cause. He mentions this calmly on the radio, along with the aliens, the zoo, the actress who shared his glass room, and the listeners laugh or write angry letters, and his daughter, hearing the broadcast played back to her by a neighbor, decides that her father has gone senile and begins quietly removing his checkbook, his car keys, his say in his own life.

He was born small and strange in a town that smelled of foundries, and grew into a boy his father could not make into a man by ordinary methods, so his father threw him into the deep end of a pool and watched him sink, and the boy discovered at the bottom that he did not mind staying there. This is the same discovery he makes years later in a snowy field behind enemy lines, when he asks the scout dragging him forward to simply leave him, and the scout beats him instead, calling him useless, weak, a coward who wants to die sitting down. The scout will die of gangrene on a train packed with prisoners, blaming him with the last of his breath, and somewhere in that packed car a young man hears the accusation and decides, without hurry, that he will one day arrange the debt's collection.

In the camp that follows there are enemy officers fat on a clerical mistake, drawing double rations year after year while the new prisoners arrive gaunt and diminished, and none of it seems to mean anything, cause without effect, effect without cause. He is moved on to a city, housed with the others in an old meat locker below a slaughterhouse, given a numbered address like livestock. The city burns in a night. He climbs up out of the cold to find it gone, ash where streets had been, and for days afterward he and the others dig bodies out of flooded cellars until one man, digging, is taken by the dry heaves and does not stop until he dies of them.

He comes home and collapses into a hospital bed, where another patient, amused by his blankness, hands him novels by a hack science fiction writer, paperbacks with lurid covers, and something in their looseness with time appeals to him before he can say why. He marries the daughter of a man who owns an optometry school and becomes rich without particularly trying to. He survives a plane crash in the mountains that kills no one else aboard, and his wife, driving frantically to reach the hospital where he lies, dies quietly of carbon monoxide leaking into her sealed car, a smaller and stranger accident than his.

He says he was taken then, or perhaps before, or perhaps it hasn't happened yet in any order that matters, to a planet where he was kept in a zoo beside a film actress, the two of them watched through glass, and where his hosts told him what he has believed ever since: that every moment that ever was or will be exists all at once, unchanging, and that free will is a delusion peculiar to his own small blue world. He carries this news onto the radio. He carries it into his living room, to his daughter, who takes his checkbook away out of love. He carries it, finally, to a lectern in a crowded hall, where he tells the audience exactly how and when he will die, and is, on schedule, shot dead by a man he never manages to see clearly, fulfilling a promise made decades or minutes or centuries ago on a train full of the dying, in a moment that, he would say, has always been happening, is happening now, and will happen again.
